2.3 Learning Methodologies 
2.3.1 Cognitive Load, Self-Regulated and Self-Determination 
Learning Theorems 
Literature review by (Brame, 2016) focuses on educational videos, they propose 
three key principles for effective learning: cognitive load, student engagement 
and active learning. 
Cognitive load as defined by (Sweller, 1988; Brame, 2016), is a theory whereby 
during the learning experience a student will observe and retain a limited 
amount of information. Initially this information is stored in short-term working 
memory, a reduced subset of that information will later be stored in a long-term 
memory. The quantity and quality of information moved into long term storage 
can be enhanced by processing the information while it is in the working 
memory in the following ways. 
1. Increasing intrinsic load – defines the amount of interconnectivity with 
pre-existing knowledge and schemas (de Jong, 2009). For example, 
programming has a high intrinsic load, since you need to understand how 
a part fits in with all the other parts of the program, whereas translating 
a single word might have a low intrinsic load since there is no other 
information suggesting that should be the case. 
2. Moderating germane load – is this stage of the learning experience where 
the student will create schemas; this is done by the student interpreting, 
classifying, and differentiating information (de Jong, 2009). If this load 
becomes too high schemas may be created that do not directly contribute 
to the desired learning outcome (de Jong, 2009; Brame, 2016).
